ai_summary:
The Reshoring American Manufacturing Act of 2026 would require the Small Business Administration's Office of Manufacturing and Trade to create and keep up a webpage to help small businesses bring manufacturing back to the United States. Onshoring means moving the making of products that a U.S. company currently produces overseas back to domestic production.

The webpage must include contact information for the relevant SBA offices and partner organizations. It must also offer a free tool that helps small businesses find organizations that could help them bring their manufacturing home. The office may add any other information it considers appropriate.

This bill directs Medicare's administrator, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), to create specific billing codes for the parts of ultralightweight manual wheelchairs. At least two codes must be set up for the wheelchair's base: one for bases made with titanium or carbon fiber, and one for bases made without those materials.

Under the bill, suppliers would still receive the same Medicare payment for these wheelchairs that would otherwise apply. If the wheelchair actually costs more than that payment, suppliers may charge the person receiving the wheelchair the difference. CMS may also require suppliers to tell beneficiaries that they could be responsible for paying that extra amount.

This bill would let the National Taxpayer Advocate hire its own lawyers inside the Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS), the office that helps taxpayers with problems involving the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). These lawyers would report directly to the National Taxpayer Advocate. The bill would also widen the National Taxpayer Advocate's power to take personnel actions. Currently that power covers the local taxpayer advocates, one located in each state. Under the bill, it would cover any employee of TAS.

Right now, a Treasury Department order puts nearly all lawyers who give legal advice to Treasury officials into the Treasury Legal Division, under the General Counsel's supervision. There are only limited exceptions. The bill would change that for TAS's lawyers. TAS is part of the IRS, which is itself part of the Treasury Department.

This bill would let people who receive money from a court judgment, award, or settlement for a sexual act or sexual contact leave that money out of their taxable income, so they would not owe federal income tax on it. Punitive damages, which are extra damages meant to punish the wrongdoer, are not covered by this exclusion.

Right now, damages can be tax-free only when they come from a physical injury or physical sickness. The Internal Revenue Service generally reads "physical injury" to mean harm you can see, such as bruises, cuts, swelling, or bleeding. The bill would remove that requirement for sexual-misconduct damages, so the money could be tax-free even if there are no medical records or visible injuries.

The bill also shifts the burden of proof in a tax dispute. If the judgment, award, or settlement says the damages are due to a sexual act or sexual conduct, the IRS would have to prove in court that the money should be taxed. In other words, the IRS would bear the burden of showing otherwise rather than the taxpayer having to prove the exclusion applies.

Finally, the bill requires the IRS to inform the public that damages related to any sexual act or sexual contact can be excluded from gross income.

This bill would let 403(b) retirement plans, the plans set up for certain workers at public schools, charities, and churches, invest in two additional kinds of investment vehicles. The first is collective investment trusts, which pool money from many investors and are held by a bank or trust company. The second is insurance company separate accounts.

The Department of Energy Nuclear Transparency Act would require the Department of Energy to publicly post information about certain nuclear facility decisions on a public website within 72 hours of those decisions or actions taking place.

The posted information would cover agreements to authorize nuclear facilities in Hazard Category 1, 2, or 3. These categories are based on how much radioactive material a facility holds and how much harm it could cause to the public, workers, and the environment, with Hazard Category 1 representing the greatest potential harm.

The Department would also have to post a summary of any steps it took to change a directive or safety standard that applies to these facilities.

In addition, the Department would be required to post any preliminary documented safety analysis or documented safety analysis it issues for these facilities. A preliminary documented safety analysis is prepared during the design and construction of a new facility, or a major change to an existing one, and gives a reasonable basis for concluding preliminarily that the facility can be operated safely. A documented safety analysis is a written review of how safely a facility can operate with respect to workers, the public, and the environment.

Finally, the Department would have to issue an annual report describing what it did to authorize these nuclear facilities during the previous year.

The 504 Modernization and Small Manufacturer Enhancement Act of 2026 would expand the Small Business Administration's 504 Loan Program, which helps small businesses pay for expansion or modernization through loans that go through a certified development company.

The bill adds new public policy goals that can qualify an intermediary for assistance. These goals include workforce development through work-based or work-integrated training, and helping revitalize an area where a disaster has been declared or determined.

It also lets intermediaries take certain steps to help close 504 loans. These include correcting borrower or lender information on loan documents and reallocating up to 10% of a project's cost.

In addition, the bill lets small businesses lease a larger share of renovated buildings financed with 504 loans to other tenants in some cases. For a project that renovates or rebuilds an existing building, a small business could lease up to 66% of the building to commercial or residential tenants if certain conditions are met. One example condition is that the small business must have occupied the building for 12 consecutive months before the project.

Finally, the bill exempts intermediaries from having to show they cannot get credit elsewhere before receiving 504 loans.

The American Enrichment Deployment Act would let a uranium enrichment facility be built before the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) issues it a license. Right now, a company needs an NRC license before it can begin construction on this kind of facility. Under the bill, enrichment facilities would be treated the same way as other nuclear fuel cycle facilities, such as those that convert uranium or fabricate fuel. They would still need an NRC license to handle special nuclear material and source material.

The bill also requires the NRC to issue or revise its regulations to carry out the law within 180 days of enactment.

The Nuclear Advisory Committee Reform Act changes how the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards, which advises the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, works. Under the bill, the committee could decline to review certain license applications issued by the NRC, such as applications for commercial nuclear power plants.

The committee could turn down reviews of license applications for commercial, industrial, medical, or research and development purposes if it decides the applications do not contain issues that are unique, novel, or noteworthy, or do not raise issues that warrant its review.

The bill also tells the committee to focus on issues that directly relate to reactor design, are important for safety, are new, and have not already been acted on by the committee.

The NRC would be directed to keep or change its policies so the committee can act efficiently and on time.

Finally, the bill requires that the committee's members have a range of technical expertise relevant to the NRC's mission.

This bill tells the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to license future U.S. facilities that recycle spent nuclear fuel, which is radioactive waste, under the rules for special nuclear material instead of the rules for production and utilization facilities. It covers domestic facilities that reprocess spent nuclear fuel in a way that does not isolate plutonium. These recycling facilities would turn spent fuel into materials that can be reused as nuclear fuel to generate electricity.

No commercial reprocessing facilities currently operate in the United States. The bill sets which regulatory framework the NRC must use for future facilities by leaving them out of the legal definition of a production facility.

The licensing process under the special nuclear material rules has fewer steps than the process under the production and utilization facility rules.

This bill moves responsibility for overseeing how foreign medical schools are accredited from the Department of Education to the Department of Health and Human Services. The work in question is done by the National Committee on Foreign Medical Education and Accreditation, which judges whether the accreditation standards used for foreign medical schools are comparable to those used for U.S. medical schools.

The bill transfers all of the Department of Education's powers and duties over this committee that it held before the bill takes effect. It also moves the staff and funding tied to these responsibilities to Health and Human Services. The bill notes that the Department of Education had already announced, on November 18, 2025, an agreement with Health and Human Services to help run the committee, including providing expertise, arranging meetings, and managing technology systems.

The bill gives the Office of Management and Budget a role in the transfer. That office must make sure the change does not increase the number of full-time equivalent employees at either department, and it must certify compliance with the bill to specified congressional committees.

Finally, the transfer does not affect any lawsuits, proceedings, or applications for benefits, services, licenses, permits, certificates, or financial assistance that are pending when the bill is enacted.

The Protecting Domestic Mining Act of 2025 would let federal agencies speed up the environmental review of certain mining infrastructure projects. It would make these projects eligible for expedited review under the Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act (the FAST Act) on a permanent basis.

The bill would give lasting legal backing to rules that already allow this. A rule issued by the Federal Permitting Improvement Steering Council (the Permitting Council) on January 8, 2021, added mining as a sector eligible for this expedited process.

The bill also would stop the Permitting Council from finalizing a separate proposed rule issued on September 22, 2023. That proposal would narrow the types of mining projects eligible for expedited review, and among its changes, it would limit the process to critical minerals mining projects.

The Fair Credit Reporting Reseller Accuracy Act would require a company that resells consumer credit information to take reasonable steps to make sure the credit information it passes along is as accurate as possible. These companies don't keep their own credit databases. Instead, they collect a person's credit information from other credit reporting agencies, combine it, and provide it to someone else.

The bill also says that a reseller cannot be held liable under the Fair Credit Reporting Act for information it passes along if it accurately reports what it received from another consumer reporting agency.

The Credit Access and Inclusion Act of 2025 lets people and the Department of Housing and Urban Development report positive credit information, such as paying rent or utility bills on time, to consumer reporting agencies. This covers payment behavior under a home rental lease or under a contract for a utility or telecommunications service.

Information about how much someone uses a utility or phone service can be reported only if it relates to the consumer's payments for that service or other terms of the service.

An energy utility company cannot report a customer's unpaid balance as late if the company and the customer have agreed to a payment plan and the customer is keeping up with that plan.

Certain existing rules that make those who provide information to consumer reporting agencies legally liable do not apply to violations of this bill.

The Government Accountability Office must report on how this kind of reporting affects consumers and on the effects of reporting consumers' cash flow data to consumer credit agencies.

The HEIRS Act of 2025 directs the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to fund grants that help people deal with the legal steps involved in inheriting certain real estate. The bill covers two grant programs.

The first program provides grants to states that have adopted the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act (UPHPA) or a similar state law. That law protects people who inherit property without a will from having their property forced into a sale. Under older state rules, such heirs became tenants-in-common, meaning any one of them could ask a court to split up or sell the property. State and local governments receiving these grants must use the money to help residents pay for costs of proving ownership or settling an estate. Those costs include title reports, title abstracts, copies of public records, land surveys, estate planning, heirs searches or tracing services, and recording, filing, notary, and legal fees.

The second program provides grants to housing counseling agencies, legal services clinics at colleges and universities, and qualified nonprofits. These groups must use the money to offer housing counseling, legal help, and financial assistance for clearing titles and keeping homes for people who inherit property as tenants-in-common.

This bill lets people who work for registered securities brokers get paid for their services through their own personal businesses, without those businesses having to register with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). It does this by exempting certain "personal services entities" from the SEC's broker rules.

Right now, anyone who handles securities trades for others must register with the SEC and join a self-regulatory organization (SRO). Under the bill, a personal services entity is a business set up by a registered representative, meaning someone who works for a broker and is registered with the appropriate SRO, to receive pay for that work from the broker. The representative is treated as an associated person of the broker.

Such an entity is not considered a broker for SEC purposes when it receives payment from the broker on the representative's behalf, as long as several conditions are met. The broker must approve the payment and keep records of it. The entity must not present itself as a broker or take part in broker or dealer activity. The broker must supervise and control the representative adequately. The broker and the entity must have a written agreement covering their relationship and how pay is handled. The entity must be owned by the representative, the representative's family, or similar entities.

The personal services entity must keep certain records and provide them to the SEC and the appropriate SRO when asked.

This bill limits how personal information about people in the securities market can be collected for tracking market activity. Specifically, it bars the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) from requiring a national securities exchange, a national securities association, or a member of either of these to hand over such information to meet the reporting rules of the Consolidated Audit Trail, which is the data regulators use to track market activity.

The NDO Fairness Act makes it harder for the government to get a nondisclosure order, which is a court order that stops a company from telling a customer that the government has asked for their emails, records, or account information. Under current law, companies that store electronic communications generally cannot share that kind of information, but the government can compel them to hand it over during an investigation, and it can also ask a court to keep the company quiet about it.

The bill raises the standard the government must meet to get or extend one of these orders. Before a court can issue an order, it must put in writing that the standard was met, based on specific and articulable facts, and it must review the warrant, order, or subpoena behind the request. Any order must also be narrowly tailored.

Most nondisclosure orders would be limited to 90 days. The exception is investigations into offenses involving child pornography or the sexual exploitation of children, where an order may last up to one year.

The bill also requires the Department of Justice to publish a report each year on how these orders are used. The report must include the number of customers or subscribers targeted, the number of applications, and how many orders were granted, extended, or denied. It must also cover orders aimed at members of the media or at certain protected activities.

This bill would require the Department of Justice to set up a task force, program, or similar structure within its Criminal Division. Its job would be to investigate and prosecute crimes related to international trade.

This bill says that a religious organization's beliefs or practices about marriage, sexuality, or gender identity cannot be treated as inconsistent with public law or policy when deciding whether the organization qualifies as a charity and so is exempt from federal income tax.

Under current federal rules, a charitable organization generally has to be organized and operated for a tax-exempt purpose, such as religious, charitable, scientific, or educational purposes, to get tax-exempt status and to receive tax-deductible donations. The Internal Revenue Service's position, which the Supreme Court upheld in Bob Jones University v. United States, is that an organization does not meet this requirement if it is against public policy or illegal.

The bill changes how that test applies to these particular beliefs. It says a religious belief or practice about marriage, sexuality, or gender identity may not be treated as inconsistent with public law or policy when deciding whether an organization is organized and operated for a tax-exempt purpose. The bill also says a belief does not have to be required by, or central to, a religion to count as a religious belief.

This bill would make certain tax-exempt organizations pay federal taxes and penalties, and in some cases lose their tax-exempt status, if they give money to a political entity within two years of receiving a contribution or gift from a foreign national. Such a payment is called a "disqualified political committee contribution" in the bill.

The bill covers organizations described in Section 501(c) of the Internal Revenue Code, which include charities, social welfare groups, labor organizations, and business or civic leagues. For the first disqualified contribution, the organization would owe a federal tax equal to 100% of the amount contributed. For each later contribution, the tax would be 200% of the amount.

For a third and each later disqualified contribution, the organization would also lose its tax-exempt status for two years, counting from the date the contribution was made.

Certain 501(c) organizations would also face a penalty equal to twice the amount of any disqualified contribution. This applies to organizations that had gross receipts of $200,000 or more, or assets of $500,000 or more, in the prior tax year.

The Foreign Funding Transparency Act would require certain tax-exempt organizations to report to the IRS how much money they receive from foreign nationals. It covers organizations recognized under Section 501(c) of the tax code, such as charities, social welfare groups, labor unions, and business or civic leagues, but only if they meet either of two thresholds: gross receipts of $200,000 or more in the previous tax year, or assets of $500,000 or more at the end of the previous tax year.

Organizations that already file a Form 990 information return with the IRS would have to report two things: the total amount of contributions they received from foreign nationals during the tax year, and the portion of those contributions that came from foreign nationals from China, Iran, Korea, or Russia.

An organization could generally accept a donor's statement about their nationality. However, it could not rely on that statement if it knows, or should know, that the statement is false.

This bill protects the right of college students to form or join social groups, including groups that admit only one sex. It applies to students at colleges and other higher education institutions.

The bill also limits what colleges that receive federal student aid can do. A college cannot take action against a single-sex social group, or against students who belong to or want to join one, just because the group admits only one sex. A college also cannot require or pressure students or group members to give up these protections, including as a condition of enrolling.

Finally, a college cannot place recruiting limits on a single-sex social group that it does not place on other student groups. The only exception is when the group and the college have signed a written agreement allowing that limit.

The Crow Tribe Water Rights Settlement Amendments Act of 2025 changes an earlier water rights agreement between the Crow Tribe of Montana and the state of Montana. That agreement was approved by the Crow Tribe Water Rights Settlement Act of 2010, which allowed the Bureau of Reclamation to plan, design, and build two major water projects on the Crow Reservation: the rehabilitation and improvement of the Crow Irrigation Project, and a municipal, rural, and industrial water system for the reservation.

The new bill updates that earlier law in several ways. It replaces references to the single water system with references to "MR&I Projects," a broader term covering more than one project. It creates a nontrust, interest-bearing account called the Crow CIP Implementation Account, so the Bureau of Reclamation can keep working on repairing and improving the irrigation project.

The bill also sets up a new MR&I Projects Account. The tribe must use money from this account only for activities related to water production, treatment, or delivery infrastructure.

Finally, the bill extends by five years, to 2030, the period during which the tribe has the exclusive right to build hydropower facilities at the Yellowtail Afterbay Dam in Montana.

This bill directs the Office of Space Commerce to set up a Commercial Space Activity Advisory Committee. The committee's job is to advise on privately run space activities and on ways to help the U.S. commercial space sector grow and stay innovative.

Among its other duties, the committee must identify challenges facing the U.S. commercial space sector. It must also review good practices that commercial space companies can follow to avoid harmfully contaminating the Moon and other celestial bodies, and to avoid negative effects on Earth's environment from material coming from space.

The committee must include members from different fields who have significant experience in the commercial space industry. It will end ten years after it is set up.

The Northern Border Security Enhancement and Review Act requires the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to regularly study threats along the northern U.S. border. The study must be done every three years. It must look at threats from terrorism and crime, recent changes in the number of people apprehended, and what improvements are needed to prevent terrorism and reduce crime.

DHS must also update its northern border strategy by September 2, 2026, and then every five years after that. The updated strategy must use the results of the latest threat study. In addition, DHS must give a classified briefing to the appropriate congressional committees.

Finally, the bill directs U.S. Customs and Border Protection's Air and Marine Operations (AMO) to create performance measures. These measures will judge how well AMO is securing the northern border between official ports of entry, both in the air and on the water.

This bill creates a government task force focused on unlawful robocalls, meaning automated phone calls that are illegal, when they come from outside the United States. The task force's job is to advise federal agencies and Congress on how to fight these calls.

The bill also changes how often the Federal Communications Commission must choose the industry group that traces the source of suspected illegal robocalls. Right now, the commission must ask industry groups to apply for that role every year. Under the bill, it would only need to ask once every three years.

This bill asks the Department of the Interior to carry out a special resource study of three archaeological sites in Illinois: Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site in Collinsville, the Emerald Mounds in St. Clair County, and the Pulcher Mounds in Monroe and St. Clair Counties. The National Park Service uses these studies to decide whether a site should become a National Historical Site.

The study has to look at several things. It must judge how nationally important the area is, and whether it would make sense and be practical to make it part of the National Park System. It must also consider other ways the area could be protected, explained, and cared for, such as through other government bodies or nonprofit groups. For each of these other options, the study must estimate what it would cost the federal government to buy land, build facilities, provide explanations for visitors, and run and maintain the site.

When the study is finished, the Department of the Interior must report its findings and give recommendations to the specified congressional committees.

This bill requires the U.S. Forest Service to transfer about 24 acres of land in the Dixie National Forest to Brian Head Town in Utah. Any buildings or other improvements on the land would go to the town along with it.

The town would have to use the land for a public works facility or for any other purpose the town decides is necessary. The land would be handed over for free, with no payment required from the town.

The Wabeno Economic Development Act would require the Forest Service to sell about 14 acres of federal land in the Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest in Wisconsin, along with the minerals underneath it, to Tony's Wabeno Redi-Mix, LLC. The sale would go ahead only if the company makes an offer to buy the land.

The Forest Service would first have to determine the land's market value through an appraisal. The company would need to submit its offer within 180 days after federal approval of that appraisal. As a condition of the sale, the company would have to pay the full market value of the land plus all costs connected to the transfer.

The bill also would require the Department of the Interior to publish a comprehensive review of the federal permitting processes used to develop stone, sand, and gravel on federal lands.

This bill directs the Forest Service to transfer certain lands within the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest in Arizona to Navajo County and Apache County. The land must be used as cemeteries.

Each county must cover all costs connected to its transfer, including the cost of surveys and environmental reviews.

This bill asks the Department of Energy to support the development of new kinds of geothermal energy systems, such as closed-loop systems that operate under supercritical conditions. It changes and adds to existing geothermal programs created under the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007, covering research and development, grants, and data management.

The Department of Energy must support a program of research, development, demonstration, and commercial use for these next-generation systems. It may use grants to carry out certain focus areas of that program. It must also make sure at least one Frontier Observatory for Research in Geothermal Energy (FORGE) field research site can handle testing of next-generation geothermal systems.

The department must also provide grants to continue and expand research, development, demonstration, testing, and commercial work at FORGE sites. Another grant must go toward setting up a next-generation geothermal systems center of excellence.

Separately, the department must provide grants to speed up the development, testing, and adoption of new technologies that make geothermal energy projects using next-generation systems more ready for commercial use.

The bill also requires the department to expand its collection of geothermal drilling information so that it includes publicly available underground data, including data reported in connection with fossil fuel and mining operations. The department must update this collection regularly to make it more useful and easier to use.

Finally, the bill allows the Department of the Interior to arrange for drilling of supercritical geothermal exploration boreholes in certain areas. These boreholes would provide reference points for mapping underground heat and developing geothermal energy.

summary:
American Franchise Act
This bill explicitly states that, for purposes of requirements under the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) and the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 (FLSA), franchisors are only considered to be joint employers with their franchisees if they regularly exercise direct and immediate control over the terms and conditions of employment for a franchisee's employees (e.g., directly hiring or firing employees on a regular basis). (The NLRA provides for collective bargaining rights in the private sector. The FLSA provides for a minimum wage, overtime pay, and other standards for employment.)
Specifically, the bill provides statutory authority for a 2020 rule by the National Labor Relations Board, particularly in relation to franchisors and franchisees. Under this rule, an entity is considered a joint employer of a separate employer's employees under the NLRA only if the entity exercises substantial, direct, and immediate control over one or more essential terms or conditions of employment. Essential terms or conditions of employment are defined to mean wages, benefits, hours of work, hiring, discharge, discipline, supervision, and direction. (In 2026, the board reinstated the 2020 rule as the applicable standard.)
The bill explicitly applies this standard to franchisors and franchisees and additionally specifies conduct that does and does not meet this standard (e.g., a franchisor setting a franchisee's operating hours does not sufficiently indicate direct and immediate control over the hours of work of a franchisee's employees). The bill also applies this standard to franchisors and franchisees under the FLSA.

ai_summary:
This bill would say that franchisors, the companies that license their brand and business model, count as joint employers of a franchisee's workers under federal labor law only in limited cases. Under the bill, a franchisor is a joint employer under the National Labor Relations Act and the Fair Labor Standards Act only if it regularly exercises direct and immediate control over the terms and conditions of a franchisee's employees, such as regularly hiring or firing them.

The bill puts into law a 2020 rule from the National Labor Relations Board. Under that rule, a business is a joint employer of another company's workers only if it has substantial, direct, and immediate control over at least one essential term of employment. The essential terms are wages, benefits, hours of work, hiring, discharge, discipline, supervision, and direction. The board reinstated this rule as the governing standard in 2026.

The bill applies this test specifically to franchisors and franchisees and spells out some examples. For instance, a franchisor setting a franchisee's operating hours does not by that fact alone show direct and immediate control over the hours that the franchisee's employees work. The same standard also applies to franchisors and franchisees under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

The CLARITY Act of 2025 sets up a set of rules for "digital commodities," which the bill defines as digital assets whose value depends on a blockchain. Under the bill, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission would generally oversee trading in these commodities, including the exchanges, brokers, and dealers that handle them. It also sets rules for monitoring trades, keeping records, and handling customer assets.

To be traded on an exchange, a digital commodity must meet one of two conditions. Either its blockchain must be mature, or it must be on a blockchain system that has reached decentralized control as the bill defines it. Alternatively, the commodity's issuer must file certain reports.

The bill also exempts digital commodities on mature blockchains, and those on blockchains expected to mature within certain timeframes, from registration with the Securities and Exchange Commission. This exemption applies if the commodity's annual sales are below a set amount and other requirements are met. At the same time, the SEC would keep authority over certain digital commodity activities and transactions carried out by some brokers and dealers on alternative trading systems and by national securities exchanges.

Digital commodity exchanges, brokers, and dealers would also have to follow the Bank Secrecy Act, which is aimed at preventing money laundering and related crimes.

Finally, the bill includes requirements for alternative trading systems and for digital commodities that were issued earlier. It also provides for provisional registration until the bill is put into effect.

This bill, the Battery Recycling for America's Competitive Economy Act (the BRACE Act), changes how lithium-ion batteries are regulated under federal waste law. The goal is to make it easier to recycle these batteries and recover critical minerals from them.

Under the bill, certain facilities that store lithium-ion batteries before recycling them would follow the rules for large quantity handlers of universal waste. Right now, these facilities must follow the stricter rules for hazardous waste. Under the new approach, they could store the batteries without needing a special permit.

This bill would require the Department of Transportation to create a rule making AM radio a standard feature in all new passenger vehicles. AM radio is commonly used to broadcast emergency alerts, news, and entertainment, and some newer vehicles no longer include it.

The requirement would cover passenger vehicles that are made in the United States for sale here, imported into the United States, or shipped across state lines, as long as they are made after the rule takes effect. Under the rule, these vehicles would need built-in equipment that can receive and play AM stations and digital AM stations, and that equipment would have to be easy for drivers to reach.

Until the rule takes effect, any manufacturer that does not include AM radio as a standard feature would have to clearly and prominently tell buyers this. Those manufacturers also could not charge an extra or separate fee for AM radio access.

The Department of Transportation could impose civil penalties for violations of the rule, and the Department of Justice could file a civil lawsuit to stop violations. The rule, including the Department of Transportation's power to enforce it, would end 10 years after the bill becomes law.

The bill also directs the Government Accountability Office to study how emergency alerts reach the public. That study would include an assessment of AM radio compared with other emergency alert technologies in the Integrated Public Alert and Warning System, and the office would report its findings.

This bill makes it easier for people who lose money to theft or fraud to get a federal tax break. It removes the rule that personal property losses count for a deduction only when they come from a federally or state-declared disaster, or when they offset personal casualty gains.

Under the bill, a taxpayer can choose to claim a deduction for a loss from theft involving fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation in the year the loss happens, rather than the year it is discovered. The deadline for asking for a refund tied to this deduction is extended to at least one year after the loss is discovered, and the limits on how much refund can be claimed are removed.

The bill also changes retirement plan rules for people who take money out early because of these fraud losses. For those withdrawals, the 10% early withdrawal penalty is waived. The deadline for filing a refund claim is extended, and the limits on the amount of that refund are removed. Finally, the taxpayer has one year, starting the day after the theft is discovered, to pay back the early withdrawal.

The Stop Pills That Kill Act would toughen criminal penalties for making fentanyl or fake drugs. It would also require federal agencies to take action against counterfeit substances.

Right now, people who possess, make, or sell certain equipment or materials used to illegally produce fentanyl, a fentanyl-like drug, or a counterfeit substance can face a harsher penalty only if the offense involves methamphetamine. This bill would extend that higher penalty to cover fentanyl-related offenses as well.

The Drug Enforcement Administration would have to create and carry out a plan to deal with counterfeit fentanyl or methamphetamine. The plan would include law enforcement efforts as well as education and prevention work. The Department of Justice would also have to report each year on how much counterfeit fentanyl or methamphetamine law enforcement has collected and on related prosecutions.

The Taxpayer Advocate Participation Act would allow the National Taxpayer Advocate to take part in U.S. court cases about federal tax law as a "friend of the court," known as an amicus curiae. In this role, the National Taxpayer Advocate can submit a written argument, called an amicus brief, even though the advocate is not a party to the case. The bill also requires federal courts to allow these appearances.

There is a limit on what the National Taxpayer Advocate may argue. The advocate may present views only on an issue that may broadly affect certain rights of taxpayers.

Some background: the National Taxpayer Advocate heads the Taxpayer Advocate Service, an independent office within the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) that helps taxpayers solve problems they have with the IRS. The advocate also proposes administrative and legislative changes to reduce those problems. Under current law, the National Taxpayer Advocate cannot appear as amicus curiae or file amicus briefs in federal tax cases. This bill would change that.

The Combating Illicit Xylazine Act would place xylazine under the federal Controlled Substances Act. Xylazine, also called "tranq," is a sedative and pain reliever approved for use in animals that is not an opioid. The Drug Enforcement Administration has reported a rise in fentanyl being mixed with xylazine.

The bill puts xylazine, including its salts and isomers, into schedule III of the Controlled Substances Act. Schedule III drugs are considered to have less potential for abuse than schedule I or II drugs, have an accepted medical use, and carry a low or moderate risk of dependence. Other drugs in this category include anabolic steroids, buprenorphine, and ketamine.

Under the bill, making, selling, or giving out xylazine, or having it with the intent to do any of those things for illegal use, would be subject to criminal penalties under the Controlled Substances Act. Xylazine transactions would also have to be tracked in the Drug Enforcement Administration's drug reporting system.

The bill exempts certain people and businesses from registration under the Controlled Substances Act when they possess xylazine that was lawfully dispensed by a veterinarian or pharmacy, and when it is for an animal or for certain animal-control or wildlife programs. It also exempts xylazine manufacturers from the act's physical security requirements.

Finally, the bill requires the Drug Enforcement Administration, working with the Food and Drug Administration, to report on how widespread illegal xylazine use is in the United States and how much it harms people. It must also provide updated information on how common xylazine trafficking and misuse have become.

This bill raises the rank of the head of the Indian Health Service inside the Department of Health and Human Services. The person who now leads the Indian Health Service would instead hold the title of Assistant Secretary for Indian Health within that department.

The GPO Modernization Act of 2026 updates how the Government Publishing Office (GPO) and the Library of Congress (LOC) operate. The bill also changes one LOC publishing requirement.

The bill makes several changes to the Federal Depository Library Program, which gives the public long-term access to federal publications. It updates the program's legal references so they cover government information in all formats, including digital. It also removes the requirement that a depository library keep a certain minimum number of books.

The bill also requires the GPO's Superintendent of Documents to create descriptive catalog records for government public information, and those records must include metadata. The Superintendent must also protect the privacy of people who use the digital repository system.

On GPO operations, the bill renames the Joint Committee on Printing, which oversees GPO, as the Joint Committee on Publishing and updates the related legal references. It states that GPO may provide publishing services and allows GPO to accept gifts. It raises the legal threshold for simplified purchases by GPO, and it updates rules on employee leave carryover and pay.

Finally, the bill changes how the Library of Congress publishes the Constitution Annotated. Instead of printing hardbound versions of the Constitution Annotated and its supplements, the LOC must prepare digital versions and publish them online. This new requirement applies to the supplement covering the Supreme Court term beginning October 2026 and to all later editions.

This bill approves a land swap between the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation, also known federally as the San Manuel Band of Mission Indians, and the federal government. The tribe's reservation is near Highland and San Bernardino in California.

If the tribe offers to transfer about 1,460 acres of its land to the federal government, the Forest Service must accept that offer and give the federal government's roughly 1,475 acres of National Forest System land to the tribe. The Forest Service must complete the transfer as soon as practical, within 120 days after it receives the offer.

As a condition of the exchange, within 120 days of the bill becoming law, the tribe must reach an agreement with the Forest Service to protect the historical and cultural character of the Arrowhead landmark site. That site sits in the foothills of the San Bernardino Mountains, directly above the city of San Bernardino.

Land the Forest Service receives in the exchange will become part of the San Bernardino National Forest.

This bill would temporarily require the Department of the Interior to give a grant to the National Law Enforcement Officers Memorial Fund. The money would pay for running and expanding the National Law Enforcement Museum's programs in three areas: community outreach, public education, and officer safety and wellness.

This bill lets the National Park Service extend long-term leases of federal property inside national parks without going through competitive bidding, but only if two conditions are met. First, the lessee must have signed the lease at least five years before the extension takes effect and must be following the lease's terms and conditions. Second, the National Park Service must decide that extending the lease is in the best interests of managing that park unit.

This bill would move ownership of certain federal lands in Nevada to state and local governments and other public bodies, mainly for economic development, recreation, or other public purposes. The land would come from the Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management and would go to the State of Nevada; Douglas, Clark, Pershing, and Elko Counties; Carson City, the City of Elko, the City of Fernley, and the City of Sparks; the Incline Village General Improvement District; and the Truckee River Flood Management Authority.

The bill would also set aside specific federal land parcels as wilderness, adding them to the National Wilderness Preservation System.

In addition, the United States would give up its reversionary interest in the Jean Prison site. This means the State of Nevada could use that land for purposes other than a prison.

The bill would allow the Department of the Interior and the Forest Service to set up a federal complex in Nevada on certain federal lands. The complex could house offices or headquarters for the Bureau of Land Management, the Forest Service, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the Bureau of Reclamation, and the Bureau of Indian Affairs.

Finally, the bill would take certain land into trust for the Washoe Tribe of Nevada and California.

This bill would require the authorized monument honoring Medal of Honor recipients to be placed within "the Reserve," the central open area of the National Mall. The Reserve is the great cross-shaped axis that generally runs from the Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial and from the White House to the Jefferson Memorial.

This bill would require the Internal Revenue Service to set up a fellowship program to recruit qualified data scientists. It would also create a task force that includes these fellows. The task force would help with several areas: choosing which tax returns to audit and how well audits work, efforts to deal with tax evasion involving offshore accounts, the use of artificial intelligence and data analysis in running the tax system, and various training and education programs.

The bill defines a qualified data scientist as a professional who has shown skill in using advanced data analysis, statistical modeling, or machine learning in complicated rules, finance, or compliance settings. These professionals would be expected to work alongside tax law specialists and other tax experts.

This bill directs the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to create a national plan to address epilepsy, with the goal of preventing, diagnosing, treating, and curing the condition. As part of that plan, HHS would coordinate research and services across all federal agencies and seek public comments.

The bill also requires HHS to set up an Advisory Council on Epilepsy Research, Care, and Services. This council would report to HHS and Congress every two years with an evaluation of the federally funded efforts on epilepsy.

In addition, HHS must send Congress a yearly report with recommended actions, based on its assessment of how the nation is progressing on epilepsy.

These requirements end on December 31, 2035.

This bill says that certain education loan arrangements do not count as "preferred lender arrangements." A preferred lender arrangement is a deal between a lender and a college or university that receives federal funding or aid, where the lender offers loans to the school's students and the school recommends, promotes, or endorses that lender's loan products.

Under the bill, arrangements made under a state-based education loan program are not treated as preferred lender arrangements for purposes of certain required disclosures to student borrowers.

This bill is meant to help rural areas, and areas with too few maternity doctors or facilities, handle obstetric emergencies, which are urgent problems that can happen during pregnancy and childbirth. It creates and expands federal grant programs run by the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA).

Under the bill, HRSA must set up a grant program for certain hospitals, or groups that include hospitals, in rural areas or areas with maternal health care shortages. The money can be used for training, building up the workforce, and buying equipment needed for obstetric emergencies.

The bill also requires HRSA's Alliance for Innovation on Maternal Health Capacity program to give grants for training on emergency obstetric care. These grants are for health care workers in rural facilities that do not have a dedicated obstetric unit.

Finally, HRSA must start a pilot program that gives grants to government entities. The money is for creating or improving telehealth programs, which let patients get care remotely, so that rural facilities without a dedicated obstetric unit can provide urgent maternal health care.

This bill extends the life of the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom through fiscal year 2028. The commission is an independent federal body that keeps track of how religious freedom is treated in countries around the world. It also reviews U.S. government policy on the issue and offers recommendations on what the government should do.

This bill, the SAFE Drugs Act of 2026, tightens oversight of compounded drugs, which are medicines mixed or altered to fit a patient's needs. Right now these don't need FDA approval, provided certain requirements are met, and there are extra limits on compounded drugs that are essentially copies of drugs already sold commercially.

Under the bill, a compounded drug counts as essentially a copy if it contains any active ingredient found in a commercially available drug, and no change made for an individual patient creates a significant difference between the two. The FDA's current definition also considers dosage strength and how the drug is given.

The bill raises the number of times a licensed pharmacist or physician may compound a drug that is essentially a copy of a commercially available drug to 20 times per month. Current FDA policy allows four such prescriptions per month.

The bill also requires physicians, facilities, and pharmacies, except hospital-based pharmacies, that compound certain drugs for out-of-state patients more than 20 times per month to file reports each year. In addition, certain large-scale outsourcing facilities, which are FDA-registered and make compounded drugs in bulk, would face regular inspections and reporting requirements.

The Biosimilar Red Tape Elimination Act would treat every biosimilar approved by the Food and Drug Administration as interchangeable with the brand-name biological product it is based on. A biosimilar is a biological product, such as a drug or vaccine, that is very similar to a brand-name version called the reference product.

Under current law, a biosimilar can be labeled interchangeable only if it meets extra requirements. That label lets a pharmacist, depending on state law, swap in the interchangeable biosimilar when filling a prescription for the reference product. The first biosimilar to earn interchangeable status for a given reference product also gets a period of marketing exclusivity.

The bill removes the extra requirements, so all licensed biosimilars would count as interchangeable. The FDA issued draft guidance in 2024 that would make some of these requirements optional, including studies on the safety of switching between a biosimilar and the reference product, but that guidance has not been finalized.

The change would take effect 60 days after the bill is signed into law, and biosimilars already licensed would be treated as interchangeable on that date. The exclusivity period still applies to first interchangeable biosimilars approved before the bill becomes law. For example, a biosimilar approved after the bill takes effect would not be treated as interchangeable with a reference product while an existing biosimilar for that product is still within its exclusivity period.

This bill asks the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) and the Forest Service to sign a memorandum of understanding with the New Mexico Land Grant Council. The agreement would describe the current steps that land grants-mercedes can take to get approval for historical, traditional, or other uses of federal land.

Land grants-mercedes were created when Spain and Mexico gave land to communities or individuals. When the United States took over the land, including New Mexico, it set up a process to review and recognize these property rights. Through that process, most of the land tied to these grants became federal land. New Mexico currently recognizes 27 community land grants-mercedes as political subdivisions.

Before entering the agreement, the BLM and the Forest Service must consult with Indian tribes.

The agreement must provide for closer cooperation and coordination between the BLM, the Forest Service, and qualified land grants-mercedes. It must also allow separate agreements with certain land grants-mercedes for specific projects.

The bill also specifies what the agreement must describe, including the procedures for giving notice and accepting public comments on land management planning decisions.

Finally, the BLM and the Forest Service must include a section in their land use plans that evaluates how other uses allowed in the plan could affect historical or traditional uses by land grants-mercedes.

The Secure Space Act of 2025 would stop the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from approving satellite licenses, ground station approvals, or permission for foreign-licensed satellites to operate in the U.S. when the applicant is a specified foreign entity of concern or one of its affiliates. Ground stations are earth-based radio sites that communicate with satellites, and market access lets a foreign-licensed satellite talk to one or more U.S.-licensed ground stations.

More specifically, the FCC could not grant any of these approvals to an entity, or to an affiliate of one, that makes or provides communications equipment or services the government considers an unacceptable risk to U.S. national security. The FCC keeps a list of these equipment and services, called the Covered List. Companies such as Huawei Technologies Company and ZTE Corporation are examples of providers whose equipment and services fall under this category.

The Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act of 2025 would place about 204.14 acres of land in El Dorado County, California, into trust for the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians.

To make this possible, the bill cancels a specified public land order and moves the land from the Forest Service to the Department of the Interior. That public land order had set the land aside for use by the Forest Service as an experiment station.

The bill directs the Department of the Interior to take two groups of land into trust for the tribe. The first is about 85.3 acres of federal land managed by the Bureau of Land Management, which includes the land moved over from the Forest Service. The second is about 118.84 acres of land the tribe already holds in fee. Together these add up to about 204.14 acres, and they will become part of the tribe's reservation. The bill also bans gaming on the land placed in trust.

This bill would ban the import, making, sale, resale, or introduction into interstate U.S. commerce of connected vehicles, along with their related software and hardware, when they are associated with China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea. A connected vehicle is one that has built-in networked hardware and software allowing it to communicate with other networks or devices through methods such as wireless connections. A vehicle counts as connected even if that communication feature is turned off or removed when it enters the country, as long as it was designed or built with that ability.

Right now, the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) already restricts transactions involving vehicle connectivity hardware and software made by companies owned, controlled, or directed by China or Russia. The bill would widen those rules to cover all four countries, instead of only China and Russia. It would also specify that certain artificial intelligence components fall under the ban.

By January 1, 2027, BIS must publish a list of items that are allowed to be imported, made, sold, resold, or introduced into U.S. interstate commerce, even though they would otherwise be covered by the ban.

The bill also includes enforcement measures. BIS must impose civil penalties on anyone who violates the prohibition.

This measure renames Chiricahua National Monument in Arizona as Chiricahua National Park. It also asks the National Park Service to protect the park's traditional cultural and religious sites and to make sure members of Indian tribes can reach those sites for traditional cultural and customary uses.

If an Indian tribe asks, the Park Service may temporarily close specific areas of the park to the general public so that tribal members can carry out traditional cultural and customary activities there. Any closure must cover the smallest area practical and last only as long as needed for those traditional cultural and religious activities.

The Western Wildfire Support Act of 2025 is meant to help the country deal with wildfires by funding recovery work after fires, encouraging the use of new technology, and requiring federal agencies to work together more closely.

On recovery, the bill gives legal authority to Burned Area Emergency Response Teams, which coordinate efforts to stabilize burned land and plan for erosion control. It also sets up an account to pay for federal rehabilitation projects in areas hit by a wildfire, such as restoring ecosystems and replacing infrastructure that land management depends on.

The bill also covers disasters of all types. It adds post-disaster help to the federal disaster preparedness program and allows federal assistance to states that run websites with information about recovery resources.

To improve wildfire management with technology, the bill directs federal agencies to speed up the permitting and use of wildfire detection tools such as sensors and cameras. It provides money to Indian tribes for slip-on tanker units, which turn ordinary vehicles into fire engines. It also calls for research into using drones in wildfire response, and studies of radio communication systems, tools that help responders understand what is happening, and computer models that predict how wildland fires will behave. In addition, it sets up a prize competition to reward new technology for managing wildfire-related invasive species.

Finally, the bill asks federal agencies to plan and coordinate better. They must use the best available science and planning tools when setting fire management policies for federal lands. They must also work with state agencies to help each other fight fires, including paying states back for fires caused by military operations. The bill further requires a study of training gaps that keep local firefighters from being fully integrated into wildfire response.

This bill would require the Department of the Interior to grant a right-of-way through the Blue Ridge Parkway, allowing an additional emergency exit from Wintergreen in Nelson County, Virginia. The grant is not automatic. Interior must first report to the specified congressional committees that three things have been completed.

The first is a review of other ways out of Wintergreen that would not cross federal land. This review must include checking whether existing trails could be converted into roads.

The second is an analysis of how a fire would likely behave around the proposed exit if an emergency occurred there.

The third is any reviews required under two federal laws: the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 and the National Historic Preservation Act.

Once Interior has reported that all three steps are done, it must grant the right-of-way.

The National Prescribed Fire Act of 2025 would require the Department of Agriculture and the Department of the Interior to conduct more controlled, planned fires on federal lands, with the goal of reducing wildfire risk.

For 10 years, each agency would need to make sure that the total area where prescribed fires are carried out grows by 10% compared with the year before.

The departments would also set up a collaborative program that gives money to eligible groups to carry out prescribed fires in priority areas. They could sign cooperative agreements or contracts with states, Indian tribes, counties, cities, fire districts, nonprofit organizations, and private companies to help coordinate these fires on federal land.

To build up the workforce, the departments would expand job opportunities for people who do prescribed fire work. This includes increasing hazard pay, supporting groups that are underrepresented in the field, and opening more training centers.

Because more prescribed fire could affect public health and safety, the Environmental Protection Agency would work with state, tribal, and local air quality agencies to support environmental reviews of wildland fires.

This bill approves a land swap between the Chugach Alaska Corporation, an Alaska Native regional corporation in southcentral Alaska, and the federal government.

If Chugach offers to transfer to the Department of the Interior all of its rights to the underground (subsurface) estate on about 231,000 acres within one year of the bill becoming law, Interior must accept that offer. In return, the federal government would transfer to Chugach all of its rights to about 65,374 acres of fee simple land in the Chugach region. The Chugach region includes parts of the Kenai Peninsula and the coast of Prince William Sound.

The bill also says that Chugach must leave out of its transfer to Interior any land, up to a total of 209 acres, where a village corporation has kept development rights (other than timber rights) or where the land has been set aside for a shareholder homesite program.

The Moab UMTRA Project Transition Act of 2025 would let the Department of Energy give the Moab site to Grand County, Utah, at no cost once the department finishes cleaning up the uranium mill tailings, which are radioactive waste, at the site. The Moab site is a former uranium milling location about three miles northwest of Moab, Utah.

The Department of Energy would keep certain water rights it needs to carry out its responsibilities. For example, it would keep access to wells and the surface area around them if cleaning up the groundwater is still underway when the site is handed over.

The transfer would have to include a condition that stops Grand County from passing any part of the land it receives to a private company or nonprofit organization.

The Gateway Partnership Act would let the National Park Service sign a one-time agreement with the Gateway Arch Park Foundation to host private events at the Gateway Arch National Park in St. Louis, Missouri, and its buildings, such as the Arch Visitor Center and the Old Courthouse. The agreement could last up to five years.

The bill sets out the terms the agreement must include. Any private event held at the park or its buildings has to fit the park's purposes and work alongside the park service's programs. Events cannot damage the park's integrity, appearance, or purposes, and they cannot be scheduled at times or in places that stop or disrupt the public from using or getting to the park or its buildings.

The park service must charge a fee to cover the wear and tear caused by private events. It can also recover all costs connected to those events, including maintenance, utilities, administrative expenses, security, and staff time.

The park service's authority to make and carry out this agreement with the foundation ends seven years after the bill becomes law.

This bill gives the National Fraud Enforcement Division, which is part of the Department of Justice, a legal basis in statute. The division's job is to investigate and bring cases against fraud that targets taxpayer money and government programs funded by taxpayers.

The division was first set up by the Department of Justice in April 2026.

This bill would stop federal money under the Higher Education Act of 1965 from going to any public college or university that treats religious student groups unfairly. A school would lose that funding if it denies a religious student group any right, benefit, or privilege that it gives to other student groups. The rule applies when the denial is based on the group's beliefs, practices, speech, leadership standards, or standards of conduct.

The Fit Future Act would give the President's Council on Sports, Fitness, and Nutrition a permanent legal basis in federal law. This council is a federal advisory group that makes recommendations on physical education in schools and on promoting good nutrition and fitness. The President most recently re-established it through an executive order on July 31, 2025.

Under the bill, the council would have to recommend fitness goals for young people. It would also suggest ways to encourage schools to reward excellence in physical education, and campaigns that highlight American sports, military readiness, and health traditions. In addition, the council would have to recommend how to bring back the Presidential Fitness Test, which sets fitness benchmarks for specific exercises based on a person's age and gender. These duties match what the executive order already requires.

The bill says the Department of Health and Human Services must provide the council with funding, administrative help, and technical support. The council may also accept money from the National Fitness Foundation.

This bill asks the State Department to strengthen how the U.S. Foreign Service is managed and how it operates. A main goal is to build up "expeditionary diplomacy," meaning diplomats who work face to face with people in high-risk places outside the embassy. It also creates new ways to hire people into the Foreign Service and adds more training requirements.

Several specific steps are included. The State Department must set up a team to create a plan for making Foreign Service members and leaders more able and willing to do expeditionary diplomacy. It must also start a program to recruit qualified veterans and military personnel who are leaving service, including by bringing Foreign Service recruiting into military transition programs. In addition, it must run a pilot program for a Diplomatic Reserve Corps, a group of trained reservists who could provide extra staff during foreign affairs emergencies. The pilot is meant to test whether this approach is practical and effective.

The bill also lets the State Department create a structured training system that fits into normal career advancement, with protected time set aside for training, similar to the professional military education used by the armed forces.

Some rules apply to Foreign Service members directly. They must complete specified leadership and management training before taking on leadership jobs. Those who take part in approved outside training, education, or details keep certain job protections, including the same eligibility for promotions and pay raises as colleagues who are not on such assignments. Finally, anyone who receives full-time, department-funded language training lasting more than six months must then serve at least three consecutive tours in positions that require proficiency in that language, starting right after the training ends.

The I&A Mission Reorientation Act of 2026 would require the Office of Intelligence and Analysis at the Department of Homeland Security to give intelligence support to state, local, tribal, and territorial governments and private sector groups on equal footing with the support it gives other parts of the intelligence community.

To meet this goal, the office would have to share information in both directions with its government and private sector partners and work to spot and deal with threats using intelligence capabilities deployed forward, closer to where problems arise. It would also have to make sure that the intelligence it gives Homeland Security leadership does not get in the way of its duties to those partners.

The bill further requires the office to keep up strong, ongoing work with fusion centers. These are partnerships among federal, state, local, or tribal governments that pool resources, expertise, or information to detect, prevent, investigate, and respond to criminal or terrorist activity.

Once the bill becomes law, the office would have to report to Congress on how it is carrying out these requirements.

This bill would bar anyone convicted of a sex offense against a minor from holding a leadership job with a labor union, from working as a consultant or advisor to a union, and from acting as an employer's labor consultant or representative in contract bargaining. The ban would last 13 years after the conviction or after the person is released from prison for that offense, whichever the bill sets as the starting point.

Under current law, the same 13-year ban already applies to people convicted of certain other crimes, such as robbery, bribery, burglary, murder, or rape. This bill adds sex offenses against minors to that list.

This bill requires the Office of Intelligence and Analysis (I&A) at the Department of Homeland Security to set up training programs for its new employees. All new hires must take standard entry-level training that covers federal privacy rights, civil rights, civil liberties, and information practices.

New employees in analytic positions must also be trained on intelligence community analytic standards and on I&A's mission. That mission includes bringing intelligence work together across DHS and sharing intelligence with state, local, tribal, territorial, and private sector partners.

New employees who collect open-source intelligence, meaning information from publicly available sources, must also receive training. That training covers the principles of collecting and managing open-source data, including how to find sources and use data in line with federal law and policy. It also covers intelligence community standards for open-source collection and related DHS authorities.

The bill also directs I&A to develop specialized training courses, including training on raw intelligence release authority, to improve its operations and support employees' professional growth. I&A must regularly give employees a list of specialized training offered by other intelligence community elements and the Department of Defense, and it must set up a system to track whether employees complete their training.

Finally, the Government Accountability Office must report to Congress on how these requirements are carried out. The report must compare the training I&A develops with the training provided by other intelligence community elements and the Department of Defense.

This bill changes how the federal government helps communities prepare for disasters through building codes, and it creates a new program to help homeowners make their homes stronger against natural hazards.

First, it makes the rules for disaster prevention aid more flexible. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) can already give pre-disaster mitigation money to government groups that adopt the newest building codes and standards, and it must consider whether a government has adopted those codes when deciding who gets this aid. The bill says that the codes that count for this purpose are the two most recently published editions, meaning either the current one or the one before it.

Second, the bill stops a type of loan from being used for building code work. Under FEMA's Safeguarding Tomorrow Revolving Loan Fund program, states and tribal governments can lend money to local governments, including for setting up and carrying out building codes. The bill removes that option, so these loans can no longer be used for building code activities.

Third, the bill creates a pilot program to help individual homeowners. FEMA would give grants to government groups, which would then pass the money on to individuals for home upgrades that make their homes more resilient to local natural hazards. People receiving the money must show they have financial need. FEMA may use up to 10% of the pre-disaster mitigation funds it provides each year to run this program, and the pilot ends at the end of fiscal year 2030.

The GOOD Act, short for the Guidance Out Of Darkness Act, sets rules for how government agencies publish their guidance documents. Under the bill, an agency must post each guidance document online on the day it is issued. It must also keep all of its guidance documents that are currently in effect in one place on a designated website, and place a link on its main website that leads to that collection.

If a guidance document is no longer in force, the agency must make that clear on the website by marking it as rescinded. The documents must be labeled as guidance and sorted into subcategories so they are easier to find.
